Informally, the '''Fourier extension operator''' is an [[Operator (mathematics)|operator]] that takes a function defined on the surface of the unit sphere in <math>\mathbb R^n</math> and applies the [[inverse Fourier transform]] to produce a function on the entirety of <math>\mathbb R^n</math>.

== Definition ==
Formally, it is an operator <math display="inline">g \mapsto \widehat{g \, d\sigma}</math> such that <math display="block">\widehat{g \, d\sigma}(x) = \int_{S^{n-1}} e^{ix \cdot \xi} g(\xi) \, d\sigma(\xi)</math>where <math>d\sigma</math> denotes surface measure on the unit sphere <math display="inline">S^{n-1}</math>, <math display="inline">x \in \mathbb R^n</math>, and <math display="inline">g \in L^p(\mathbb R^n)</math> for some <math display="inline">p \ge 1</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Bennett |first=Jonathan |last2=Nakamura |first2=Shohei |date=2021-06-01 |title=Tomography bounds for the Fourier extension operator and applications |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00208-020-02131-0 |journal=Mathematische Annalen |language=en |volume=380 |issue=1 |pages=119–159 |doi=10.1007/s00208-020-02131-0 |issn=1432-1807}}</ref> Here, the notation <math display="inline">\widehat{f}</math> denotes the fourier transform of <math display="inline">f</math>. In this [[Lebesgue integral]], <math display="inline">\xi</math> is a point on the unit sphere and <math display="inline">d\sigma(\xi)</math> is the Lebesgue measure on the sphere, or in other words the Lebesgue analog of <math display="inline">dx</math>.

The Fourier extension operator is the (formal) adjoint of the '''Fourier restriction operator''' <math>g \mapsto \widehat{f} \vline_{S^{n-1}}</math>, where the <math>\vline_X</math> notation represents restriction to the set <math display="inline">X</math>.<ref name=":0" />
